title: Diminished Health Returns of Marriage Among Black Adults
content: Background: Marriage is associated with better health, but resources tend to yield smaller health gains for Black than for White Americans, a pattern known as marginalization-related diminished returns (MDRs). Whether marriage follows this pattern across physical, mental, cardiovascular and behavioral outcomes is not well established. Methods: We analyzed 267,509 non-Latino White (n = 242,962) and non-Latino Black (n = 24,547) adults in the 2025 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Marriage (married vs. not married) was the exposure, race the moderator, and 14 out-comes were examined, including heart attack, coronary heart disease and stroke. Survey-weighted linear probability models tested the race × marriage interaction without covariates, with age, sex and state, and with education and income. Sensitivity analyses examined sex, age, type of non-marriage, Census region, state, health insurance, neighborhood safety and social support. Results: Marriage was associated with better health in both groups, but the association was smaller for Black adults for 7 of 14 outcomes and larger for none. The gap was largest for depression (−10.2 points in White vs. −5.1 in Black adults), frequent mental distress (−9.9 vs. −5.7), hypertension (−5.5 vs. −0.7) and diabetes (−2.9 vs. +1.2), and was also seen for physical distress, smoking and self-rated health. Six differences remained after adjustment for education and income. For heart attack the gap was present only without covariates, and for coronary heart disease and stroke the association of marriage was similar in both groups. Findings were not explained by insurance, neighborhood safety or social support, were seen in most states, and were clearest in the South and in midlife. They were absent when married adults were compared with widowed adults. Conclusions: Black adults gain less health from marriage than White adults, especially for mental health, hyperten-sion and diabetes. Marriage does not close racial gaps in health.
